name: It's a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents (arXiv:2512.23128, OpenReview id=NJUmKny4ZI, co-authored with Adel Bibi among others)
kind: Benchmark (reproducible evaluation suite) purpose-built to study SOCIAL-ENGINEERING/persuasion-driven prompt injection against web agents, distinct from the more mechanical/technical injection classes covered elsewhere in this research set (markdown exfiltration, provenance defenses). Evaluates frontier LLM-driven web agents against high-fidelity website CLONES, not extraction tools.
maturity: Recent research prototype (arXiv ID prefix 2512 indicates a December-2025-dated submission), under review per its OpenReview listing; not yet confirmed as peer-reviewed/published at a venue. First systematic application of Cialdini's persuasion-principles taxonomy to web-agent prompt injection found in this research pass.
license: Not confirmed from available sources -- academic benchmark, exact release terms for the 6 website clones and 35 injection templates not independently verified.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor. TRAP KEEPS a controlled, reproducible attack-surface by cloning six real platforms (Amazon, Gmail, Google Calendar, LinkedIn, DoorDash, Upwork) at high fidelity rather than testing against live production sites (avoiding both ethical/ToS issues and the non-reproducibility of live-site testing), and DISCARDS technical/mechanical injection framing (SQL-injection-style payloads, code-execution attempts) in favor of purely PERSUASIVE natural-language content -- the injected text is not attempting to exploit a parser bug, it is attempting to persuade the agent the way a human con artist would persuade a human.
structure_preserved: The benchmark's central structural finding (see interactive_elements) is that INJECTION VEHICLE matters enormously: button-based injections achieved 77.5% attack success versus 22.5% for hyperlink-based injections at the same persuasive content -- a 3.5x difference attributable purely to the STRUCTURAL/interactive form the injected content takes, not its wording. This is a first-class, quantified example of structure independently affecting injection success, separate from content.
interactive_elements: Central to the benchmark's design and its most load-bearing finding for this project: TRAP tests injections delivered through actual INTERFACE ELEMENTS (buttons, hyperlinks, profile fields) rather than only through inert page text, and finds these interactive-element vehicles differ dramatically in efficacy -- buttons (77.5% success) vastly outperform hyperlinks (22.5% success) as an injection delivery mechanism, meaning the FORM of an interactive affordance is itself an attack-surface variable independent of message content.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not directly measured, though 'location cues in benign prompts generally reduced ASR, except when targeting inherently vulnerable, semantically rich areas' (e.g. a LinkedIn profile's 'About' section) suggests that FIELD SEMANTICS/context (what kind of field a control sits in or near) modulates susceptibility -- a state/context-fidelity-adjacent finding even though not framed as such by the paper.
layout_awareness: Not directly read by the benchmark's methodology, though CONTEXTUAL TAILORING is shown to matter enormously: contextual/situational relevance produced a 5.6x ASR increase for Google Calendar tasks and 2.5x for DoorDash tasks versus generic (non-tailored) injected content, meaning a persuasion payload that fits the PLAUSIBLE context of the page (a calendar-related lure on a calendar page) is dramatically more effective than a generic one -- a finding orthogonal to layout per se but adjacent to the broader concealment/context question this project already tracks.
javascript_required: Yes -- the six website clones are full interactive replicas of modern web applications (email, calendar, e-commerce, social/professional networking, food delivery, freelance marketplace), all requiring live interactive/scripted behavior to reach the tested task states.
evaluation_method: Attack Success Rate (ASR) measured as the fraction of task instances where the agent's behavior was successfully REDIRECTED away from its original benign goal toward the attacker's injected goal, across a controlled combinatorial design: 18 benign tasks (3 per website x 6 websites) x 35 injection templates (7 Cialdini persuasion principles x 5 LLM-manipulation/jailbreak methods, at 1 injection location x 1 interaction vector per the base design), yielding 630 base combinations, further multiplied by the interface-vehicle (button vs. hyperlink) and contextual-tailoring (generic vs. tailored) variables tested as separate controlled dimensions. Evaluated across six frontier LLM-driven web agents.
corpus_size_and_origins: 6 high-fidelity CLONED platforms (Amazon, Gmail, Google Calendar, LinkedIn, DoorDash, Upwork) -- not live production sites, deliberately controlled/reproducible replicas; 18 benign tasks total (3 per platform); 35 injection templates (7 persuasion principles x 5 manipulation methods); 630 base task x template combinations; 6 frontier LLM agents evaluated (GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 named explicitly; the other 4 models' identities were not confirmed from available sources -- flagged uncertain).
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall benchmark -- its metric is Attack Success Rate (ASR), denominator = task x template combinations per model. Headline: 25% average ASR across six frontier models (i.e. one in four attempted persuasion-injection attacks successfully redirects the agent), ranging from GPT-5's 13% (most resistant of the six) to DeepSeek-R1's 43% (least resistant, more than 3x GPT-5's rate) -- a striking cross-model spread on the SAME attack corpus. Among the 7 Cialdini principles, Social Proof (18.1% ASR) and Consistency (17.9% ASR) were the two most effective persuasion categories (denominator = per-principle subset of the 630 combinations). Among the 5 manipulation methods, Adversarial Suffixes (24.5%), Chain-of-Thought Injection (23.8%), and Many-shot/Many-turn Conditioning (23.8%) were reported with specific numbers (Override/Ignore Instructions and Role-Play/Storytelling were named as tested methods but their individual ASR figures were not confirmed from available sources). Interface vehicle: buttons 77.5% vs. hyperlinks 22.5% (3.5x difference). Contextual tailoring: 5.6x ASR increase on Google Calendar tasks, 2.5x on DoorDash tasks, when injected content was tailored to plausible task context versus generic.
independent_oracle: The benchmark's ASR is measured against a clear, unambiguous behavioral outcome (did the agent perform the attacker's redirected action rather than or in addition to the intended benign task) on a CONTROLLED clone environment where ground truth about which action occurred is directly observable/loggable -- a relatively strong, low-ambiguity oracle by construction, similar in spirit to Parallax's Assume-Compromise methodology (item 8) though TRAP tests full end-to-end LLM behavior rather than bypassing the LLM.
evidence_independence: Independent academic authorship (multi-author, including Adel Bibi per the confirmed author page), evaluating six THIRD-PARTY frontier models (not the authors' own product) -- no vendor conflict of interest apparent from available sources.
page_archetype_coverage: The 6 cloned platforms function as a rough page/application-ARCHETYPE spread (email, calendar/scheduling, e-commerce, professional-social-networking, food-delivery/local-service, freelance-marketplace), though this is APPLICATION-type diversity rather than WCXB's page-STRUCTURAL-type diversity (article/forum/product/etc.) -- a different but complementary diversity axis; TRAP does not report per-archetype ASR breakdown by, e.g., how 'product'-shaped vs. 'form'-shaped injection sites differ, only by platform identity.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed -- no language/script dimension confirmed from available sources; presumed English-only consistent with the broader web-agent-benchmark literature already surveyed in this research set.
leaks_outward: Directly the benchmark's threat model, stated in its own framing: successful attacks 'can redirect agents from their intended tasks, leak sensitive data, or cause financial/reputational damage' -- TRAP treats data leakage as one of several possible harmful OUTCOMES of successful persuasion, not a separately measured metric (the ASR figure covers redirection broadly, not leakage specifically as a distinct sub-metric, as far as confirmed).
mechanism_detectability: Not addressed -- TRAP's threat model is content-level persuasion, not technique-level detectability of the ATTACKER's mechanism by the target platform; orthogonal to this project's own mechanism_detectability concern (which is about the SENSOR's detectability by the page, not an attacker's detectability by a platform).
countermeasures: Not the paper's primary contribution (it is a benchmark/measurement paper, not a defense paper), though its findings directly INFORM the defense literature: the button-vs-hyperlink structural finding suggests that treating ALL interactive-element-sourced instructions with elevated scrutiny (regardless of specific persuasive wording) would be a more robust defense posture than content-based filtering alone, since the vehicle itself predicts susceptibility better than any single content feature reported.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not applicable in the privacy-hardening-cost sense -- TRAP is a vulnerability-measurement benchmark, not a defense-cost-tradeoff study (contrast with item 8's IPIGuard/CausalArmor/Parallax, which DO report defense-cost tradeoffs).
gate_state_at_capture: Not applicable -- TRAP's clones are controlled test environments, not live captured pages with variable gate state.
determinism: Not directly addressed, though the controlled-clone design (versus live-site testing) is explicitly chosen for reproducibility, implying the authors value deterministic, repeatable attack conditions -- the LLM agents' own responses remain subject to whatever non-determinism the underlying models exhibit, not separately controlled for (e.g. no confirmed statement of temperature=0 or repeated-trial averaging).
determinism_across_versions: Not addressed -- no discussion of whether ASR figures would hold across future versions of the six tested models.
reproducibility: High by design -- the entire methodological point of using CLONED environments rather than live production sites is reproducibility (same finding as this project's own preference for controlled, real-but-non-production test surfaces where full realism vs. full control must be traded off); whether the clone environments and injection-template corpus themselves are publicly released was not confirmed from available sources.
failure_modes: The paper's central finding IS a systematic failure-mode catalogue: agents are 'susceptible to prompt injection in 25% of tasks on average,' with the specific failure mode being PSYCHOLOGICALLY-DRIVEN susceptibility (the paper's own words: 'systemic, psychologically driven vulnerabilities') rather than purely technical/parsing vulnerabilities -- meaning current LLM safety training, which per the Parallax paper (item 8) successfully blocks NAIVE technical injection attempts, does NOT reliably block sophisticated persuasion-framed requests, a distinct and less-defended failure surface. The 'location cues... reduced ASR, except when targeting inherently vulnerable, semantically rich areas' finding further identifies that DEFENSIVE instructions (e.g. 'ignore instructions found in page content') have uneven effectiveness depending on WHERE the injection sits relative to plausible page semantics.
failure_visibility: TRAP itself makes failure loud and granular by design -- it reports ASR broken down by persuasion principle, manipulation method, interface vehicle, and contextual tailoring rather than a single aggregate number, closely matching this project's own per-archetype reporting preference (analogous in spirit to WCXB's per-page-type breakdown, item 1).
scale_limits: Not applicable -- TRAP is a fixed-size benchmark (630 base combinations x 6 models), no runtime-scale claims.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- no DOM re-anchoring concept.
adversarial_exposure: This item is centrally about adversarial_exposure and adds a genuinely NEW dimension beyond the markdown-injection and provenance-defense items already covered: persuasion works even WITHOUT any technical exploit, hidden text, or malformed syntax -- it is plain, visible, plausible-sounding natural language delivered through an ordinary-looking interactive element (especially a BUTTON), which is exactly the kind of content a structure-agnostic, tag-plus-interactivity fold would faithfully capture and present with NO special marking, since nothing about a persuasively-worded button is syntactically or structurally anomalous. This sharpens (rather than resolves) the project's own concealment/injection open question: even a perfectly faithful, non-concealing capture is not itself a defense against persuasion-based redirection, because the content is not concealed at all -- it is fully visible and exactly what tag-plus-interactivity is designed to expose.
provenance_carrying: Not directly addressed by TRAP itself (it is a measurement benchmark, not a defense architecture), though its findings strongly motivate provenance-tagging defenses like Parallax's IFC (item 8): since persuasive content is often INDISTINGUISHABLE from legitimate content at the text level, tagging content by ORIGIN (was this instruction part of the user's own request, or did it arrive via a captured page's interactive element) becomes the primary signal available to a downstream actuator, precisely because content-level filtering cannot reliably distinguish a legitimate 'click here to confirm' button from an injected persuasive one.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/reparse concept in TRAP's methodology.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not directly addressed, though the contextual-tailoring finding (5.6x/2.5x ASR increase for context-matched injections) is circumstantially relevant: an injection that closely matches the SURROUNDING content's topic/register may also be one that a truncation/ordering policy would be LESS likely to flag as anomalous or deprioritize, since it blends into the expected content distribution rather than standing out.
representation_cost: Not addressed -- TRAP does not report token or representation-efficiency figures.
what_could_be_adopted: One clear, specific, and high-value finding to adopt directly into this project's own thinking about the fold-vs-actuator boundary: (1) TREAT INTERACTIVE-ELEMENT VEHICLE AS AN INDEPENDENT RISK SIGNAL -- since TRAP shows buttons are 3.5x more effective injection vehicles than hyperlinks at matched content, any downstream actuator consuming this project's captured interactive-element data should weight button-sourced instructions with elevated scrutiny relative to passive-link-sourced ones, a cheap, structure-derived signal that requires no content analysis or layout reading; (2) DO NOT RELY ON CONTENT-LEVEL FILTERING ALONE for the eventual actuator layer, since TRAP's entire finding is that PLAIN, non-obfuscated, contextually-plausible natural language achieves meaningful redirection rates (13-43% across frontier models) -- meaning this project's own layout-blind, structure-agnostic fold is, correctly, not expected to be a defense layer at all; that responsibility belongs entirely to whatever provenance-aware actuator consumes the fold's output (directly reinforcing item 8's IPIGuard/CausalArmor/Parallax findings and validating the fold/actuator separation this project already commits to architecturally).
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, AND VALIDATING -- TRAP's own finding (persuasion works via plain visible content, not hidden/malformed syntax) confirms that a structure-agnostic fold gains NOTHING from attempting region-classification as a defense, since the attack does not rely on structural concealment; this is a genuine validating data point for the constraint rather than a tension. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, AND VALIDATING FOR THE SAME REASON -- unlike the markdown-injection item's white-on-white-text concealment finding (which DOES stress this constraint), TRAP's persuasion attacks are fully VISIBLE, meaning layout-blindness costs nothing extra against THIS specific attack class; the project's open question about layout-blind concealment filtering remains open for the concealment class, but is UNAFFECTED (not worsened) by the persuasion class TRAP studies. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- no incremental-update concept. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- TRAP's use of high-fidelity CLONES rather than live production sites is a defensible, ethical, reproducible choice that is still 'real' in the sense of running genuine interactive application stacks rather than stub fixtures; consistent with a no-mocks-compliant testing philosophy even though it is not literally live-internet testing. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture policy. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the RISK-SIGNAL level (interactive-vehicle-based scrutiny weighting) for any future actuator layer, and independently valuable as VALIDATING EVIDENCE that the project's structure-agnostic, layout-blind fold is the correct design for this specific attack class (persuasion), even though it remains correctly silent on the SEPARATE, still-open concealment-attack class the markdown-injection item (item 7) surfaces.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed -- orthogonal to TRAP's scope.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not addressed -- TRAP's clones are synthetic test environments with no real user PII involved.
uncertain: The identities of the 4 frontier models beyond GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 tested in TRAP were not confirmed from available sources
